books.proposedTitle: The Secret of the Harbour Compass

chapters.title: The Boat and the Secret Compass
paragraphs: Emma stopped so suddenly that Max bumped into her shoes. In the harbour shop stood a little wooden boat with a purple sail. ‘Six pounds,’ said the shopkeeper. Emma checked her purse. Four pounds. Her smile slipped.

Then the brass compass on her backpack gave a tiny click. Its needle spun towards the harbour, though Emma was standing still. ‘Max, did you see that?’ Max wagged his tail as if he had been waiting all morning.
At home, Emma and her grown-up counted four one-pound coins. ‘Two more pounds to reach six,’ Emma said. ‘We can make a plan,’ her grown-up replied. ‘And you can change your mind later.’
Emma drew the boat in her notebook. She wrote WAIT beside it. Outside, a gull cried three times. The compass clicked again. This time its needle pointed towards the bakery.

chapters.title: The Bakery's Invisible Payment
paragraphs: At the bakery, the warm bread smelled so good that Max sat down at once. Emma watched a customer place coins on the counter. Another customer tapped a card. ‘But where did the money go?’ Emma whispered.
‘The coins are cash,’ said her grown-up. ‘A debit card pays using money in a bank account. It does not make new money.’ Emma looked at the card reader as though it were a secret door.

The baker showed them a price tag. ‘However you pay, the bread still costs the same.’ Emma pictured money travelling from an account to the shop. ‘So tapping is still spending!’ she said. Max sneezed at a floury bag.
Behind the till, Emma noticed a little paper boat. On its sail someone had drawn the same compass symbol. She leaned closer. Written underneath were three words: CHECK BEFORE PAYING.

chapters.title: The List That Saved the Day
paragraphs: The market was buzzing. Emma saw bright toys, juicy apples and a rainbow umbrella. Max pulled gently towards the food stalls. Emma unfolded their list: bread, vegetables and soap.
‘Could we buy the purple boat instead?’ she asked. ‘We need food and soap today,’ her grown-up answered. ‘The boat is something you want. It can wait.’ Emma tucked the list safely into her pocket.

Rain began to patter. Emma pointed at the umbrella. ‘Is that a need or a want?’ ‘It depends,’ said her grown-up. ‘Someone who must walk home in heavy rain might need it.’ Emma liked that the answer was not always the same.
A gust of wind swept the list towards the harbour. Max raced after it and stopped beside a green spinning top. It whirled on a stall without anyone touching it. Emma had to look twice.

chapters.title: The Spinning Top Trap
paragraphs: Round and round went the green spinning top. ‘Only two pounds!’ called the seller. Emma felt the four coins in her purse. The top was wonderful. So was the boat with the purple sail.

‘If I spend two pounds, how much will I have?’ Emma asked. She placed four pretend counters on the bench and moved two aside. ‘Two pounds left,’ she said. ‘I cannot spend those same coins on the boat.’

The top spun faster. Max chased his own tail and made Emma laugh. She could buy the top or keep saving; both were choices. She sat quietly until the excitement settled. ‘I will wait today,’ she decided.
The seller smiled and put the top away. Under it lay a folded paper with six empty circles drawn on it. Emma picked it up. ‘That looks exactly like a saving plan,’ she said.

chapters.title: Six Circles and a Paper Sail
paragraphs: Emma drew six circles in her notebook. Each stood for one pound towards the boat. She coloured four. Two circles stayed white. ‘That is how much I still need,’ she told Max.

‘Maybe another pound will be available to save later,’ said her grown-up. ‘Maybe not. A plan can change, and nobody has to save money they need for something important.’ Emma nodded. Her notebook was a guide, not a promise.
While she waited, Emma folded a paper boat and gave it a purple sail. Max watched from his blanket as she floated it in a shallow tray. It sailed beautifully and had cost nothing.
Then Emma saw a poster through the window. A giant toy ship seemed to burst out of the paper. In enormous letters it shouted: HURRY! LAST CHANCE! Emma reached for her purse, then stopped.

chapters.title: The Poster That Shouted
paragraphs: The poster was so bright that Emma almost forgot her plan. ‘That ship looks bigger than our kitchen!’ she said. Max barked at the picture as though it might sail away.

Her grown-up helped her read the small print. The toy was much smaller than its picture. It also needed batteries that were not included. ‘An advert wants our attention,’ Emma said. ‘It does not choose for us.’
Emma asked the shopkeeper about the price and what came in the box. She could think, compare or buy nothing. The words LAST CHANCE could not make her decide. She stepped away with Max.

A sudden gust blew a picnic napkin across the path. An older neighbour was trying to catch the rest of the papers before they reached the water. Emma forgot the poster and ran to ask if they needed help.

chapters.title: The Harbour's Free Treasure
paragraphs: ‘May we help?’ Emma asked the neighbour. With her grown-up beside her, she gathered the clean papers that had blown onto the dry path. Max stayed close and carried nothing except his favourite toy.
‘Thank you,’ said the neighbour. ‘I thought my picnic was ruined.’ Emma smiled. Helping had taken time but no money. Later she drew a little boat for a friend who was feeling lonely.
‘You can be kind by listening, sharing time or helping safely,’ said her grown-up. ‘Giving money is optional. You never have to give away money you need.’ Emma put her notebook back into her bag.

The neighbour handed Emma a scrap of paper. On it was a drawing of the harbour and a question: WHAT IS WORTH MORE THAN A COIN? Emma looked at Max, her friend and the sunny water. She thought she knew.

chapters.title: The Choice at the Harbour
paragraphs: Some time later, Emma had six pounds available for her boat goal. Her grown-up agreed she could choose a toy. Together they returned to the harbour shop, where the purple-sailed boat still waited.

Emma checked its price and asked how to use it safely. Six pounds, exactly. She could buy it, save the money for later or choose something different. The compass on her backpack stayed still. This decision belonged to her.
‘I still want the boat,’ Emma said. She paid six pounds and received no change. Those coins were now spent. Back home, she floated the boat in a shallow tray while Max watched from the dry floor.

At last Emma understood the compass. It had not told her what to buy. It had reminded her to stop, think and choose. She smiled at the purple sail. Tomorrow, she might find a new adventure, with or without money.

chapters.title: The Plan Nobody Heard
paragraphs: Emma and Max arrived at the community garden with a notebook full of ideas. The children wanted to turn an empty corner into a reading space. One suggested a tall platform. Another wanted a secret ladder. Everyone talked at once.

Emma sketched the ladder while Max slept under the table. Then she noticed a child who had not spoken. The child pointed to the drawing, shook their head and reached for a communication board. Emma stopped drawing.

‘We have not heard everyone's ideas,’ she said. She moved the paper so the whole group could see it and offered pictures, writing and time to think. Silence, she realised, was not the same as agreement.

The child pointed to a picture of a tree and then to a quiet-space symbol. Emma added them to the plan. Suddenly the exciting ladder looked less certain. The team had discovered its first mystery: who had their plan forgotten?

chapters.title: The Path With a Problem
paragraphs: The next morning, Emma followed a garden volunteer along the path to the empty corner. At first it looked wide enough. Then they imagined someone using a wheelchair or walking aid trying to reach the seats.
The children asked people how they might use the space. Someone wanted a quiet place near the tree. Another needed a clear route and room beside a seat. No single person could speak for everyone.

Emma drew a broader path and a ground-level reading area. The volunteer reminded the team that adults would check access, materials and safety before any building began. A beautiful drawing was only the beginning.
Max trotted towards a patch of sunshine and sat down. ‘He has chosen his favourite spot,’ Emma laughed. But two different seat designs were still on the table, and their creators were about to argue.

chapters.title: The Great Cushion Disagreement
paragraphs: ‘Bright cushions!’ said one child. ‘Wooden seats!’ insisted another. Their voices grew louder. Emma felt her shoulders tighten. If she picked a favourite, the argument might end, but would the choice be fair?
She suggested a pause. Then she asked the group to choose the same questions for both ideas: Could people use them? Would they be comfortable? Would they work outdoors?

Cushions could feel cosy, but rain might soak them. Wooden seats might dry more easily, but the team still needed to check comfort and access. The volunteer offered to help them test a small arrangement safely.
The children agreed to try ideas rather than choose a winner. Emma wrote TEST, DON'T GUESS in her notebook. But there was a new problem: everyone wanted the same job.

chapters.title: The Job Board Surprise
paragraphs: Emma almost handed out all the jobs herself. Then she remembered the child with the communication board. ‘What would each person like to do?’ she asked instead.

They made a job board: draw signs, count materials, arrange picture labels and collect feedback. Children could choose a role, share it, ask for help or take a break. Adults kept responsibility for tools and building.
One child preferred writing to speaking aloud. Another noticed that the materials count was wrong. Emma thanked them and changed the list. Their quiet observation had saved the team from a mistake.

Max's official job was to rest safely away from the busy work area. When the trial corner was ready, the team stood back proudly. Then a visitor walked straight past it. Why hadn't they seen the sign?

chapters.title: The Sign That Hid the Garden
paragraphs: The painted sign was lovely. Golden letters curled around green leaves. But from the path, the words were too small to read. A visitor asked where the reading corner was.

Emma felt disappointed. The team had worked hard. ‘The sign isn't doing its job yet,’ she said. ‘That doesn't mean the artist did anything wrong.’ Together they tried bigger letters and a simple picture of a book.
They placed the new sign where visitors could see it without blocking the path. The original painted leaves became a border. The child who had painted them helped choose the new layout.
At last visitors found the corner. One smiled and sat down. Another looked around and asked, ‘Could there be a shaded seat too?’ Emma opened her notebook again. The adventure was not over.

chapters.title: The Garden That Kept Growing
paragraphs: On opening day, children read under the tree. Some sat. Some stood. Others used picture cards to share ideas. Nobody had to give their name or speak aloud to take part.
Emma recorded the request for shade and asked the volunteer to review it with the team. They could not promise that every idea would work, but they could listen, test and improve the space safely.
At the final meeting, Emma thanked the children who had noticed the path, compared the seats, checked the list and improved the sign. The garden belonged to everyone who had helped shape it.

Max curled up beneath the tree. Emma touched her compass badge. She had begun wanting to lead the project. Now she knew better questions: Who hasn't had a chance? What are we assuming? What should we try next?
